title: Find Missing Constants in Equivalent Expressions with Regression
description: Use Desmos regression with a list of allowed input values to find missing constants in expressions that are equivalent for every permitted value of the variable.
authoring_notes: Reverse-drift export 2026-08-26: reconstructed from the production lesson 4c22e546-2a07-4ffc-8f99-a2f3e3b21f59 (md5-verified block dump) so the repo is the source of truth again. Block ids without semantic names were authored in-app; generated ids follow block_type_N.

blocks.html:
Give it a try

Spend about a minute on this question. Keep your first idea, even if you are unsure. You can continue without submitting an answer.

shared_prompt.title: Opening question
shared_prompt.html: The expression \(z^2+az+b\) is equivalent to \((z+4)(z-3)\) for all z. What is ab?

blocks.html:
Make equivalent expressions match at several inputs

The opening question asks for constants that work for every input. Expanding can be tedious. Instead, regression can find constants that make the two expressions match at several inputs together.

We’ll start with a simple identity so you can see which letters get values and which letter gets a list.

content.hint: Read the assignments shown directly below the regression line.
content.prompt: What do a and b equal in \(ax^2+bx+6\)?
content.explanation: Desmos finds \(a=3\) and \(b=9\). Those values make \(ax^2+bx+6\) equivalent to \(3(x+1)(x+2)\).

blocks.html:
One set of constants, many inputs

Equivalent expressions have the same value at every allowed input. The constants stay fixed while the input changes. A match at just one input may not determine those constants.

Separate the two jobs

In \(a(x+2)+b\), \(x\) is the input; \(a,b\) are the missing constants. Give the input a list so Desmos compares several values.

Use \(x_1\) for input x or \(y_1\) for input y; lowercase x and y have graphing jobs. Another input such as t can keep its name.

content.hint: Which letter is allowed to vary while the missing constants stay fixed?
content.prompt: In the identity \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)=5t+10\), which letter should become a list in Desmos?
choices: \(p\), because it appears first in the identity
\(q\), because it is the subtracted constant
Both \(p\) and \(q\) at the same time
\(t\), because it is the input variable
content.explanation: The identity must work for many values of \(t\), so define \(t\) as a list. Only inputs named \(x\) or \(y\) need a subscript because those letters are reserved for graphing. Desmos will solve for the fixed constants \(p\) and \(q\).

blocks.html:
A list supplies several comparisons

At just one input, many pairs of constants might work. A list such as \(x_1=[2,3,4]\) lets Desmos compare the expressions at three distinct inputs at once.

content.hint: Think about what “equivalent for all values” means.
content.prompt: Why do you enter \(x_1=[2,3,4]\) instead of letting Desmos choose one value of \(x_1\)?
choices: Equivalent expressions must match at many input values, and one value may not determine every constant.
A list changes the two equivalent expressions into one equation with a missing constant.
Regression cannot use positive input values unless they are supplied in a list.
The SAT requires the specific input values 2, 3, and 4 for this question type.
content.explanation: Several input values force one set of constants to make the expressions agree repeatedly. The particular values are flexible as long as they are allowed.

blocks.html:
List, Match, Read

  1. Rename an input x or y to \(x_1\) or \(y_1\) throughout.
  2. Define several distinct allowed inputs in a list.
  3. Put a tilde, ~, between the expressions.
  4. Read the constants, then type the requested combination.

For exact identities, inspect RMSE for zero or a tiny mismatch. If the constants remain undetermined, add more distinct allowed inputs.

Try the complete setup

Enter \(x_1=[2,3,4]\) and \(ax_1^2+bx_1+6\sim3(x_1+1)(x_1+2)\). Read \(a,b\), then type \(a/b\) on another row.

calculator.title: Type a/b on the next line

content.hint: Use ~ between the expressions and make t—not a missing constant—the list. Since t is not reserved for graphing, it does not need a subscript.
content.prompt: Which two-line setup correctly finds \(p\) and \(q\) if \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)\) is equivalent to \(5t+10\)?
content.explanation: The regression adjusts \(p\) and \(q\) while testing the identity at \(t=0,1,2\). Only x and y need to be changed to subscripted inputs.

blocks.html:
Choose the input list

Use an explicit list when the allowed values are known, or \(x_1=[1...10]\) for consecutive allowed integers.

If a forbidden input depends on a missing constant, \(x_1=\operatorname{random}(5)\) supplies five values between 0 and 1 and makes an exact collision unlikely. Keep any other domain restrictions satisfied.

content.hint: Choose the method whose values lie between 0 and 1 and are very unlikely to equal the still-unknown value of b.
content.prompt: A denominator contains \(x-b\), so the forbidden input depends on the missing constant \(b\). Which list method is most useful before \(b\) is known?
content.explanation: \(random(5)\) creates five values between 0 and 1. When the forbidden input depends on the unknown \(b\), an exact random collision is highly unlikely.

blocks.html:
Every input must be allowed

Exclude zero denominators and respect stated intervals or square-root domains. If the expression contains \(1/(x-2)\) and x>2, use values such as \(x_1=[3,4,5]\).

content.hint: Every value must be greater than 2, and 2 itself makes the denominator zero.
content.prompt: The expressions contain \(1/(x-2)\), and the question states \(x>2\). Which list is safest?
content.explanation: The values 3, 4, and 5 satisfy \(x>2\) and keep \(x-2\) nonzero.

blocks.html:
Use the same setup with a denominator

Enter \((ax_1+b)/(x_1-2)\sim3+5/(x_1-2)\) and \(x_1=[3,4,5]\). Read \(a,b\), then type \(a-b\).

If Desmos finds the input too

If the panel shows a value for t along with the constants, it treated t as another unknown. Add the missing input list, such as \(t=[2,3,4]\). The panel should then find only the constants.

content.hint: The input variable should contain several values supplied by the student, not one value chosen by regression.
content.prompt: The regression panel displays \(a=2\), \(b=7\), and \(t=4.6\). What is the most likely setup mistake?
choices: The student used too many allowed values.
The student already calculated the requested expression.
The student forgot to define \(t\) as a list.
The student should replace \(a\) and \(b\) with \(x\) and \(y\).
content.explanation: Add a line such as \(t=[0,1,2]\). Then regression tests several inputs while solving only for the missing constants. Since t is not reserved for graphing, no subscript is needed.

content.title: Enter the identity and its input list

targeted_hints.message_html: You need three lines: the regression, the input list, and \(2p+q\).
Use only the regression, the input list, and \(2p+q\).
Enter all three required lines before checking your work.

feedback.retry_message_html: Use exactly three lines: the regression, \(t=[0,1,2]\), and the requested calculation \(2p+q\).
feedback.success_message_html: Good work. Desmos uses the list to find \(p=3\) and \(q=2\), then evaluates \(2p+q=8\) on the third line.

content.instructions_html: For \(p(t+4)+q(t-1)\equiv5t+10\), enter the regression and \(t=[0,1,2]\). Read \(p,q\), then calculate \(2p+q\).

content.hint: Type \(2p+q\) using the values Desmos stored.
content.prompt: What result did Desmos display for \(2p+q\) on the third line?

content.title: Build the restricted identity

targeted_hints.message_html: You need three lines: the regression, the safe list, and \(a-b\).
Use only the regression, the safe list, and \(a-b\).

feedback.retry_message_html: Use exactly three lines: the regression with \(x_1\), the safe list \(x_1=[3,4,5]\), and the requested calculation \(a-b\).
feedback.success_message_html: Nice work! Strong work. The inputs are safe, regression finds \(a=3\) and \(b=-1\), and the third line evaluates \(a-b=4\).

content.instructions_html: For the restricted identity in the prompt, enter a regression using \(x_1\) and the allowed list \(x_1=[3,4,5]\). Calculate \(a-b\).

content.hint: Subtracting a negative adds its opposite: \(3-(-1)\).
content.prompt: What result did Desmos display for \(a-b\) on the third line?
content.explanation: \(a-b=3-(-1)=4\). You built the regression, protected the domain, and answered the requested combination.

blocks.html:
Return to the missing constants

Try the opening question again. Decide which letter needs several inputs and which letters Desmos should find.

content.prompt: Return to the opening question. What answer do you get now?
content.explanation: The equivalent polynomial is z²+z-12. Thus a=1 and b=-12, so ab=-12.
content.solution: Enter z=[2,3,4] and z²+az+b~(z+4)(z-3). Desmos shows a=1 and b=-12. Their product is -12.
content.hint: Give z several input values, connect the equivalent expressions with a tilde, and read a and b before calculating ab.
Recall the five actions: regression symbol, rename x or y if needed, safe list, constant assignments, requested calculation.
content.prompt: You need constants that work for every allowed input. What setup keeps the input separate from the constants?
choices: Use =, let Desmos choose one input value on its own, and report the first constant assignment shown for the expression.
Use ~, change x or y to a subscripted input, define a list of allowed inputs, read the constant assignments, and evaluate the requested expression.
Replace each letter, constants included, with its own list, graph both sides, and read the intersection.
Use ~ with the ordinary letter x, include the forbidden input values in the list, and round the constants to integers.
content.explanation: You have it. That sequence makes the expressions match at several valid inputs and then uses the stored constants to answer exactly what the SAT asks. Inputs other than x or y keep their original names.

blocks.html:
Try it on your own

Choose the approach for each question. Try these now or save them for homework.

content.prompt: Independent practice 1 of 5: The expression \(p(t+2)+q(t-1)\) is equivalent to \(5t+7\) for all \(t\). What is \(p-q\)?
content.explanation: Matching the expressions gives p=4 and q=1, so p-q=3.

content.prompt: Independent practice 2 of 5: The expression \(a(y-3)+b\) is equivalent to \(4y+2\) for all \(y\). What is \(a+b\)?
content.explanation: The identity gives a=4 and b=14, so a+b=18.

content.prompt: Independent practice 3 of 5: An identity contains \(1/(x-b)\), where \(b\) is a missing constant, and no other restriction is given. Which definition is the best starting list while \(b\) is unknown?
content.explanation: random(5) supplies several inputs while making an exact collision with an unknown forbidden input unlikely. Keep other domain restrictions satisfied.

content.prompt: Independent practice 4 of 5: An identity contains \(1/(x+4)\), and the question specifies \(x<0\). Which input list is valid?
content.explanation: The list [-3,-2,-1] contains negative values and excludes -4, which makes the denominator zero.

content.prompt: The expression \(a(x-2)+b(x+1)\) is equivalent to \(5x-7\) for all values of \(x\). What is the value of \(a\)?
content.explanation: Matching the identity gives \(a+b=5\) and \(-2a+b=-7\), so \(a=4\) (and \(b=1\)). In Desmos, \(a(x_1-2)+b(x_1+1)\sim5x_1-7\) with \(x_1=[1,2,3]\) finds the same values; \(1\) is \(b\), the wrong quantity.

content.html:
List the inputs, find the constants

Use allowed inputs and calculate the quantity the question requests.
